name: Exterior Dry Cold invading the Lungs
pinyin: Wài Zào Liáng Hán Fàn Fèi
description: Exterior Dry Cold invading the Lungs (Wài Zào Liáng Hán Fàn Fèi, 外燥凉寒犯肺) is a full TCM pattern affecting the Lung. Key signs: Dry cough with scant or thin wa...
key_signs: ["Dry cough with scant or thin watery phlegm", "Dry and stuffy nose", "Dry or scratchy throat", "Chills with mild or no fever", "Absence of sweating", "Mild headache", "Nasal congestion", "Sensation of throat blockage", "Slight body aches", "Dry lips", "Hoarse voice", "Tickly or itchy throat triggering cough", "Dry skin", "Slight thirst with preference for warm drinks", "Fatigue or feeling run down", "Sneezing", "Slight chest tightness", "Dry eyes", "Pain between the eyebrows or forehead"]

timing_worsening_explanation: Symptoms typically appear in late autumn (after the autumn equinox through early winter), when the climate shifts to cold and dry. According to TCM seasonal theory, this is the period when cool dryness predominates. Cough and throat dryness tend to worsen in the evening and at night when temperatures drop further. The early morning may also be uncomfortable due to accumulated dryness in the airways overnight. In TCM's organ clock, the Lung is most active between 3 and 5 AM, so coughing may be more noticeable in the early morning hours.
practitioner_notes:
Diagnosing this pattern involves recognising the combination of two pathogenic factors acting together: cold and dryness. The key diagnostic reasoning centres on several observations:
First, the cough quality is revealing. Unlike a wind-cold cough that produces thin white phlegm, or a wind-heat cough with thick yellow phlegm, this pattern features a distinctly dry cough with very little or no sputum. When phlegm does appear, it is scant and thin. This dryness points to the involvement of the Dryness pathogen (燥邪), which damages the body's fluids and strips moisture from the Lung's delicate lining. Second, the accompanying signs of dryness throughout the nose, throat, and lips confirm that this is not simple wind-cold. A practitioner looks for the combination of cold signs (chills, absence of sweating, mild headache, thin white tongue coating) together with dryness signs (dry nose, dry throat, dry tongue coating) to pinpoint this specific pattern.
The seasonal context is also important. This pattern is most characteristic of late autumn, when the weather turns both cold and dry. The classical text Wen Bing Tiao Bian describes this as a time when cool dryness predominates. The overall clinical picture resembles a mild common cold but with a dry quality that sets it apart. If the same dry cough appeared with heat signs (fever, thirst for cold drinks, yellow phlegm, red tongue), the diagnosis would shift to Warm Dryness (温燥) instead, which requires a completely different treatment approach.
pathophysiology: Cool, dry autumn air invades through the nose and skin, constricting the body's surface while simultaneously depleting the Lungs' protective moisture, producing a combination of chills with dryness symptoms.
treatment_principle: Gently disperse Cold-Dryness from the exterior, restore the Lungs' dispersing and descending functions, moisten Dryness, and resolve Phlegm
typical_timeline: 3-7 days for uncomplicated cases with proper treatment; up to 2 weeks if diagnosed late or complicated by pre-existing Lung weakness
formula_modifications:
Common Modifications to Xing Su SanIf there is no sweating at all and the pulse feels very tight: Add Qiang Huo (Notopterygium root) to more strongly open the pores and promote a light sweat. The goal is just enough perspiration to release the trapped Cold from the surface, not heavy sweating.
If sweating has occurred but the cough persists: Remove Zi Su Ye (which was there to release the exterior) and add Zi Su Geng (Perilla stem) instead. The stem focuses more on regulating Lung Qi downward rather than releasing the surface, which better addresses a lingering cough after the exterior Cold has already been resolved.
If there is also diarrhoea and abdominal bloating: Add Cang Zhu (Atractylodes) and Hou Po (Magnolia bark) to dry dampness in the intestines and relieve distension. This addresses the Spleen's impaired fluid transport that sometimes accompanies this pattern.
If headache extends to the brow ridge area: Add Bai Zhi (Angelica dahurica), which specifically targets pain in the forehead and brow area by opening the nasal passages and dispersing Wind-Cold from the Yang Ming channel.
If signs of Heat begin to appear (such as mild fever or yellow-tinged sputum): Add Huang Qin (Scutellaria) to clear developing Heat from the Lungs. However, do not use Huang Qin if there is concurrent diarrhoea and bloating, as its cold nature could worsen those symptoms.

causes_details: [{"cause_title": "Exposure to cool, dry autumn weather", "explanation": "This is the most common cause. In late autumn, the air turns both cold and dry. The Lungs are considered the most 'delicate' organ in TCM because they connect directly to the outside world through the nose and throat. When a person breathes in cold, dry air, or is exposed to chilly autumn winds, the drying quality of the air depletes moisture from the Lungs' airways while the cold quality tightens the body's surface and blocks normal sweating.\nThe classical texts describe the Lungs as an organ that 'prefers moisture and dislikes dryness.' When dry-cold air enters through the nose and mouth, it directly strips away the thin layer of protective fluid that lines the respiratory passages. At the same time, the cold component closes down the pores and skin surface, trapping the pathogenic factor inside. The result is a combination of surface symptoms (chills, no sweating, mild headache) with dryness symptoms (dry throat, dry nose, dry cough)."}, {"cause_title": "Wind carrying Cold-Dryness into the body", "explanation": "Wind is considered the 'lead pathogen' in TCM. On its own, Cold-Dryness would have difficulty penetrating the body's defences. But wind pries open the surface layer (the protective Qi that circulates along the skin), allowing Cold and Dryness to ride in together. This is why the condition typically develops after exposure to a cold, dry wind rather than simply being in a cold, dry room.\nThe classical teaching that 'Wind is the chief of the hundred diseases' explains why this pattern almost always involves Wind alongside Cold and Dryness. The Wind component is responsible for the relatively sudden onset and the headache, while Cold and Dryness produce the more specific symptoms in the Lungs and airways."}, {"cause_title": "Underlying dryness or weakened Lung defences", "explanation": "Some people are naturally more prone to this pattern because their Lungs already have insufficient moisture. This can result from living in a very dry climate, working in air-conditioned environments, a history of chronic cough, or simply having a constitutionally dry body type. When such a person encounters autumn cold-dryness, the pathogenic factor meets less resistance and produces a more pronounced pattern. The dryness component hits harder because there is less fluid reserve in the Lungs to buffer it."}, {"cause_title": "Excessive intake of cold or raw foods in autumn", "explanation": "Eating large amounts of cold or raw foods (such as salads, chilled drinks, raw fruit, or ice cream) during the autumn transition further weakens the body's warming, protective functions. In TCM, the Spleen and Stomach are responsible for transforming food into warmth and nourishment. Overconsumption of cold foods slows this process and weakens the protective Qi that guards the body's surface. With diminished surface defences, cold-dry autumn weather has an easier entry into the body."}]

formulas.name: Xing Su San
formulas.description: Xing Su San (Apricot Kernel and Perilla Leaf Powder) is the representative formula for Exterior Dry Cold invading the Lungs. Created by Wu Jutong in the Wen Bing Tiao Bian, it gently disperses Cool-Dryness from the surface while restoring the Lungs' descending function and resolving thin Phlegm. Its key pair of Zi Su Ye (releasing the exterior with warmth but without excessive drying) and Xing Ren (descending and moistening Lung Qi) defines the formula's balanced approach.

herbs.name: Zi Su Ye
herbs.description: Perilla leaf (Zi Su Ye) is the chief exterior-releasing herb for this pattern. It is warm but not drying, gently dispersing Cold from the surface and restoring the Lungs' ability to spread Qi outward.

herbs.name: Xing Ren
herbs.description: Apricot kernel (Xing Ren) descends and moistens. It restores the Lungs' downward-directing function to stop coughing, while its mild moistening quality helps counter the Dryness that is depleting lung fluids.

herbs.name: Qian Hu
herbs.description: Peucedanum root (Qian Hu) assists both in dispersing exterior pathogenic factors and in directing Lung Qi downward to resolve phlegm. It bridges the formula's exterior-releasing and interior-descending actions.

herbs.name: Jie Geng
herbs.description: Platycodon root (Jie Geng) opens and lifts Lung Qi, helping to unblock the nose and throat. It pairs with descending herbs like Xing Ren and Zhi Ke to create balanced Lung Qi movement.

herbs.name: Ban Xia
herbs.description: Pinellia rhizome (Ban Xia) dries dampness and transforms Phlegm. When Cold-Dryness disrupts the Lungs' fluid distribution, moisture collects into thin watery Phlegm, and Ban Xia helps resolve it.

herbs.name: Chen Pi
herbs.description: Tangerine peel (Chen Pi) regulates Qi flow and helps dry dampness. It supports the Spleen's role in fluid transport, preventing further Phlegm accumulation.

herbs.name: Fu Ling
herbs.description: Poria (Fu Ling) strengthens the Spleen and gently drains excess dampness, cutting off the source of Phlegm production and supporting fluid metabolism.

herbs.name: Zhi Ke
herbs.description: Bitter orange (Zhi Ke) promotes the downward movement of Qi. Paired with Jie Geng, it creates an up-and-down balancing effect that helps the Lungs regain their normal dispersing and descending rhythm.

acupoints.name: Lieque LU-7
acupoints.description: Lie Que (LU-7) is the Lung channel's connecting point and one of the Eight Confluent Points (linking to the Conception Vessel). It powerfully disperses Wind and Cold from the Lung system, opens the nose, and restores the Lungs' outward-spreading function. It is the single most important point for exterior Lung conditions.

acupoints.name: Hegu LI-4
acupoints.description: He Gu (LI-4) is the source point of the Large Intestine channel (which is paired with the Lung channel). It releases the exterior, promotes sweating, and clears the head and nose. Combined with LU-7, it forms the classic pairing for any exterior pattern affecting the Lungs.

acupoints.name: Fengchi GB-20
acupoints.description: Feng Chi (GB-20), meaning 'Wind Pool', is a key point for expelling Wind from the head and neck. It relieves headache, nasal congestion, and neck stiffness that commonly accompany this pattern.

acupoints.name: Feishu BL-13
acupoints.description: Fei Shu (BL-13) is the Back Transporting point of the Lungs. It directly supports the Lungs' dispersing and descending functions, helps stop coughing, and can be combined with cupping to expel Cold from the Lung area.

acupoints.name: Fengmen BL-12
acupoints.description: Feng Men (BL-12), the 'Wind Gate', is located on the upper back near the Lung area. It is specifically indicated for Wind-Cold patterns and helps release pathogenic factors from the exterior. Cupping or moxibustion here is especially effective.
